title: MA9-03138
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: The claimant, XXXXX XXXXXX XXXXXXX XXXXX, a Mexican citizen, is claiming refugee protection in Canada under section 96 and subsection 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).
The claimant alleged that her life is in danger in Mexico, by reason of the threats received from her former boss, an individual named XXXX XXXXX.

The claimant is originally from XXXXX in the state of XXXXX. Her Personal Information Form1 (PIF) states that before her departure from Mexico, she worked at XXX XXXXXX in the city of XXXXX. She worked there from XXXXX 2007 to XXXXX, 2008, the date when she was dismissed because of a lack of work.

Her problems are due to the fact that she insisted that her former employer give her the sums of money due for salary and severance pay. In that regard, on XXXXX, 2008, the claimant contacted a lawyer to help her recover the sums of money that the employer refused to pay to her. Her lawyer, XXXX XXXXX, prepared a complaint that she filed to the Secretariat of Labour and Social Welfare in the city of XXXXX, against the company that managed the XXX. The claimant submitted under exhibits P-5 and P-62 some documents to support her complaint.
On XXXXX, 2009, the claimant went to the XXX to submit a notice to appear for the conciliation and arbitration scheduled for XXXXX, 2009.
On XXXXX, 2009, three individuals approached the claimant, who was with a female friend. They ordered her to withdraw the complaint against the company that managed the XXX, if she valued her life.

The claimant, who feared for her life, reported on XXXXX, 2009, to the Secretariat of Labour and Social Welfare, to withdraw her complaint. However, an officer told her that she could not do so because the process had already begun.

The next day, the claimant went to the office of the public ministry to file a complaint against her former boss, XXXX XXXXX, for the threats received on XXXXX, 2009. She was informed that there would be an investigation. Exhibit P-7,3 submitted to attest to her way of proceeding, indicates that a preliminary investigation was opened.

Later in the day, when she was walking on the street, two individuals approached the claimant and informed her that she must withdraw her complaint if she did not want to find herself dead. This incident took place in front of police officers who did not intervene to help the claimant.
Fearing for her life, the claimant made arrangements to leave Mexico. She left on XXXXX, 2009, the date when she arrived in Canada. She claimed refugee protection upon her arrival.
The panel determines that the claimant is not a "Convention refugee" or a "person in need of protection" under subsection 97(1) of the IRPA.

After examining the claimant's alleged reasons to support her refugee protection claim, the panel is of the opinion that the harm feared is not a product of section 96 of the IRPA. The refugee protection claim is assessed under paragraph 97(1)(b) of the IRPA, as the state is not implicated in the harm feared. The issue is whether her return to Mexico would personally subject her to the risks that are enumerated in paragraph 97(1)(b) of the IRPA.

The issues analyzed in this refugee protection claim were the credibility of the alleged facts, the state protection and the internal flight alternative in Mexico City, in Mérida in Yucatan, and in Puebla.

The evidence on file includes the PIF, the claimant's testimony and several documents submitted to corroborate the alleged facts, in particular those that resulted in her problems and the threats that she faced.
The panel is satisfied as to the identity and citizenship of the claimant. A copy of her passport, seized by Citizenship and Immigration Canada (CIC), was placed on the record.4 CREDIBILITY

Having heard the claimant's testimony, the panel finds that she provided a credible and genuine testimony with respect to the problems that she experienced in Mexico. The panel has no reason to doubt her testimony, which was spontaneous and direct. No contradiction arose between the testimony rendered and the other evidence on file.

In addition, although it was not necessary, her testimony was corroborated by several pieces of material evidence. Taking into account the exhibits submitted, in particular exhibits P-5, P-6 and P-7, the panel believes the testimony of the claimant, who stated that she submitted a complaint to the Secretariat of Labour and Social Welfare in XXXXX 2009, and that she then received death threats from her former employer, XXXX XXXXX.
The panel must determine whether the claimant discharged her burden of proof regarding state protection and internal flight alternative.
The claimant had to establish clear and convincing5 evidence of the Mexican state's inability to protect her given her particular circumstances.

There is substantial case law that has established the criteria to be applied for this. First, the state is presumed capable of protecting its citizens.6 The Federal Court has indicated on a number of occasions that claimants must make reasonable efforts to seek protection from the authorities in their country,7 without, however, putting their life in danger. The analysis of the availability of state protection cannot be done in abstract; the panel must take into account the particular facts of each refugee protection claim, in particular the claimant's and their attacker's profile, as well as the harm feared.8

In this case, the claimant stated that she reported to the office of the public ministry on XXXXX, 2009, in order to file a complaint regarding the death threats that she had received the night before. She stated that she was informed that there would be an investigation. The claimant submitted Exhibit P-73 to corroborate the steps taken at the office of the public ministry. This document clearly indicates that a preliminary investigation is open. The claimant stated at the hearing that she did not know whether the investigation had continued, because she left XXXXX on XXXXX, 2009.

The panel cannot conclude from the evidence presented that the claimant discharged her burden of rebutting, through clear and convincing evidence, the presumption that the state is capable of protecting its citizens.

Her testimony, which was found to be credible, revealed that that same day, she was approached by some men who threatened her again by ordering her to withdraw the complaint filed. When asked to specify which complaint her attackers were referring to, the claimant responded that it was the complaint at the Secretariat of Labour and Social Welfare.

The panel cannot conclude from this that the authorities and her attackers are colluding, all the more so since she was informed at the office of the public ministry that there would be an investigation. Although it is not related to state protection, the panel outlines that, when she wanted to withdraw her complaint from the Secretariat of Labour and Social Welfare, the officer told her that it was impossible because the process had begun and that it was an employer who had a prior record for labour relations.

It is generally accepted that international protection is only necessary if a refugee protection claimant cannot live safely elsewhere in their country. The evidence revealed that the claimant lived in XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, according to her counsel's statements. INTERNAL FLIGHT ALTERNATIVE (IFA)

This question was analyzed taking into account the principles set out in Rasaratnam9 and Thirunavukkarasu.10 It is a matter of assessing whether an internal flight alternative (IFA) exists for the claimant, and whether it was reasonable for her to seek refuge in locations identified as safe for the claimant. At the start of the hearing, the panel had identified Mexico City and Mérida in Yucatan. During the hearing, the evidence revealed that her mother and her son had lived in the city of XXXXX since XXXX 2010, and that they did not have problems related to the claimant. The panel questioned the claimant about the possibility of her living there, after informing her of it. First component of the IFA

The risk assessment of a claimant is of a forward-looking nature. The panel is of the opinion that, in taking into account the claimant's personal situation, she can live safely elsewhere in Mexico, in particular, in the identified locations.

During the hearing, the claimant stated that she could not live safely elsewhere in Mexico because her attacker, who works for a company that has XXX in other Mexican cities, would end up finding her with the help of the government databases.

According to the panel, the claimant's problems are the result of the complaint that she filed in XXXXX 2009 at the Secretariat of Labour and Social Welfare, in order to recover the sums of money that she was due. The analysis of the evidence indicates that the attacker wanted the claimant to withdraw her complaint.

The claimant left her country two years ago. According to her statement at the hearing, following the threats, she tried in vain to withdraw her complaint; the panel understands from her behaviour that she prefers to avoid the problems rather than follow up on her complaint. She stated at the hearing that, since XXXXX 2009, she has not received news from the lawyer who helped her in the steps taken with the Secretariat of Labour and Social Welfare.

Although the claimant was found to be credible regarding the problems experienced, the panel is of the opinion that it was pure hypotheses on her part when she stated that her lawyer, who no longer responded to her calls, probably received a bribe, to end the steps taken on behalf of the claimant.

In the assessment of the risk that the claimant would be subject to should she return to Mexico, the panel took into account that, at the hearing, the claimant stated that her mother lived in XXXXX with the claimant's son until XXXX 2010, when she retired. The claimant did not inform the panel of particular problems that they experienced in connection with her, or that they were bothered there in connection with her.

Since XXXX 2010, her mother has lived in XXXXX with her son, and they have not had any problem there either in connection with the claimant. This leads the panel to believe that it is unlikely that her attacker, who did not try to locate her at her mother's home, is still interested in her.

Mexico is a large country. It has a population of approximately 11 million,11 more than three times the population of Canada. Mexico City, Mérida and Puebla are located several hundred kilometres from XXXXX.

The literature that the panel read about the government databases12 does not enable the panel to conclude that it is likely that the claimant would be located if she sought refuge in the locations suggested as providing a viable IFA. In fact, tab 2.4 states that it is difficult to be located in Mexico with the help of the government databases: Of all the interlocutors interviewed, none was aware of incidents in which witnesses to crime and corruption were located by their aggressors through the use of government databases or registries....In particular, SIEDO's Jorge Rosas Garcia, the AFI's Beatriz Gonzalez Dominguez and the SDHAVSC's Carlos Garduno were unaware of any cases in which national registries, such as the Federal Electoral Institute (Instituto Federal Electoral, IFE) database, had been used to track individuals who had relocated to avoid detection by criminal groups....Public access to national registries, including the IFE database, is prohibited by law.13

In addition, with respect to whether the information of Mexican citizens is easily accessible, the information in tab 3.4 states that; [A]ccording to Article 135 of the Federal Code of Institutions and Electoral Procedures, documents, data and information provided by Mexican citizens to the Federal Registry of Voters is strictly confidential and cannot be divulged to anyone except authorized users within the organization.14

Lastly, tab 3.6 states that "[e]mployees with the IFE and with the Federal Registry of Voters also have limited access to the data and, if they access it without authorization, they could be subject to criminal and administrative sanctions."15

According to the panel, the simple statement that corruption exists in Mexico is not sufficient to conclude that her attacker would have access to the government databases and thus be able to locate her. According to the panel, the claimant did not establish, on a balance of probabilities, that her attacker has connections, in that he would have access to the government databases or the interest to follow her.

Taking into account the particular facts of this refugee protection claim and the evidence available, the panel is of the opinion that the claimant did not establish that it is probable that her life would be in danger in the identified locations. SECOND COMPONENT: REASONABLENESS OF THE IFA

The claimant had the burden of proving that it was unreasonable for her to live in the places identified as safe locations. The panel is of the opinion that the claimant did not discharge her burden of proving this.

The claimant is young, and she has nothing preventing her from moving elsewhere in her country. It is likely that she could find herself work in the identified locations. The panel took into account the statements of her counsel, who asked the panel to consider her situation as a single-parent mother and her personal circumstances.
However, the tribunals have indicated on several occasions that the threshold for concluding that an IFA is unreasonable is high.16

In Ranganathan,17 the Federal Court of Appeal stated that: [f]or the unreasonableness test of the IFA, a very high threshold must be set....It requires nothing less than the existence of conditions which would jeopardize the life or safety of a claimant in travelling or temporarily relocating to a safe area and it requires actual and concrete evidence of such conditions.

In this refugee protection claim, the panel does not have "actual and concrete evidence of such conditions" in the identified areas. For these reasons, the panel considers that the IFA does not "jeopardize the life or safety" of the claimant.
For these reasons, the panel is of the opinion that the claimant did not discharge her burden of proof regarding the IFA.

For these reasons, after examining the personal situation of the claimant, the panel concludes that she was unable to establish that her return to Mexico would personally subject her to the risks enumerated in paragraph 97(1)(b) of the IRPA.
Consequently, the panel determines that the claimant, XXXXX XXXXXX XXXXXXX XXXXX, is not a "Convention refugee" or a "person in need of protection" under subsection 97(1) of the IRPA.

The panel rejects the refugee protection claim.
